ideas.title: SpaceX Filed for a $2 Trillion IPO. The S-1 Describes a Satellite ISP.
ideas.trend: SpaceX filed its S-1 this week targeting a $1.75T valuation and $75B raise on Nasdaq; Starlink is 61% of revenue and the only profitable segment per CNBC's prospectus analysis
ideas.consensus: SpaceX is the most ambitious company in history: rockets, Starship, Mars, orbital internet
ideas.angle: Starlink is the cash machine ($4.42B income, 63% EBITDA); the rocketry division lost $657M; the AI division lost $6.35B; the $2T ask prices narrative (Starship, orbital data centers, Mars) on top of a satellite ISP worth ~$130B on standalone broadband multiples

content_pack.x_longform:
SpaceX filed for a $2 trillion IPO. The S-1 describes a satellite internet company.

Starlink generated $11.39 billion in revenue last year. 61% of total company revenue. The only segment that posted a profit: $4.42 billion in income with a 63% EBITDA margin. Subscriber count crossed 10.3 million, doubled from a year ago. Per CNBC's analysis of the prospectus, the connectivity unit is the only division keeping the consolidated books out of the red.

The rocketry business, NASA contracts and Department of Defense deals and Starship launches all included, lost $657 million.

The AI division lost $6.35 billion.

Total operations: $4.9 billion in losses on $18.7 billion in consolidated revenue for 2025. A $1.75 trillion valuation ask sits on top of those numbers.

Price the segments separately.

Starlink at $11.4 billion in revenue and 63% EBITDA margins is one of the best businesses built in the satellite sector. Growth-stage broadband operators with aggressive subscriber curves trade at 7-10x EBITDA. Price Starlink at the high end of that range and the math lands near $130 billion. A serious number. A defensible number. The consolidated ask is thirteen times that.

The gap between $130 billion and $1.75 trillion is narrative: Starship, orbital AI data centers the S-1 projects will begin deploying by 2028, Mars. Each item lands in the prospectus as optionality priced into today's multiple. None of it generated revenue in 2025.

The subscriber curve deserves scrutiny. The first 10 million were the high-value captures: enterprise aviation deals with United, Southwest, and Hawaiian, government contracts, affluent rural households with no broadband alternative. The next 10 million push into lower-income geographies and more contested markets. Amazon's Project Kuiper begins commercial service this year with $10 billion committed. OneWeb is operational. The premium-margin segment gets competitive faster than the headline subscriber number suggests.

The AI division warrants its own line item. $6.35 billion in losses in 2025. The S-1 does not disaggregate what those operations are building or on what timeline they become profitable. The xAI integration and orbital computing thesis appear in the filing as future bets. Public markets absorb the current burn.

Governance compounds the picture. Musk controls 85% of shareholder votes per the filing. No institutional block, no board action, no proxy campaign changes the company's direction. The 21 banks underwriting the $75 billion raise price that risk into their spreads. Public investors do not get the same hedge.

In 2006, Amazon looked like a retailer competing with Walmart on price. It was building AWS: cloud infrastructure generating 70%+ operating margins that funded every Amazon business for two decades. Investors who priced Amazon as a retailer left the cloud story on the table. The data was in the filing.

SpaceX reads as rockets. The money comes from satellites. The $1.75 trillion multiple is a bet the rest of the prospectus comes true.

content_pack.substack_draft:
The SpaceX S-1 is roughly 400 pages long. The financial picture clarifies on about page 40.

Starlink generated $11.4 billion in revenue last year, 61% of total company revenue, with a 63% EBITDA margin and 10.3 million subscribers. The rocketry business lost $657 million. The AI division lost $6.35 billion. SpaceX as a consolidated entity lost $4.9 billion from operations. The company asking public markets for a $1.75 trillion valuation is, in the financial statements, a satellite internet provider with a money-losing rocket and AI business attached.

Most people think of SpaceX as the rocket company going to Mars. The more I read the S-1, the more I realized the better analogy is Amazon in 2006: the business generating the margins is not the one on the cover. Amazon looked like a retailer; it was building the cloud infrastructure layer. SpaceX looks like a rocket company; it is running a satellite ISP with 63% EBITDA margins that is subsidizing everything else.

The difference matters for pricing. Starlink on standalone broadband multiples gets you to around $130 billion. Getting to $1.75 trillion requires betting that the orbital AI data centers, the Starship commercial market, and the Mars mission all contribute meaningfully before the subscriber curve flattens. I am not sure that bet is wrong. But I am not sure the current multiple has adequately priced the risk that one or two of those bets takes longer than the prospectus projects.

ideas.title: Anthropic Beat OpenAI to Profitability With a Command-Line Tool
ideas.trend: Anthropic projects first-ever $559M operating profit in Q2 2026 on $10.9B revenue; Claude Code at $2.5B ARR is ~23% of total revenue per WSJ/CNBC reporting
ideas.consensus: Anthropic wins enterprise AI on safety and model quality; Claude is the premium choice for careful deployments
ideas.angle: The profit is powered by Claude Code, a terminal CLI, not the enterprise API or chat interface; Claude Code crossed $1B ARR in six months and $2.5B in under a year, the fastest developer tool ramp in history

content_pack.x_longform:
Anthropic beat OpenAI to profitability. The engine is a command-line tool.

Q2 2026 revenue is projected at $10.9 billion, per figures reported by WSJ, up from $4.8 billion in Q1. That is 130% sequential growth. Expected operating profit for the quarter: $559 million. First in the company's history.

Claude Code, the terminal-based coding agent, sits at $2.5 billion in annualized revenue as of this quarter. Roughly 23% of total Anthropic revenue from a single product running in a shell. It crossed $1 billion ARR within six months of launch. Slack took four years. ChatGPT took eleven months. Claude Code did it in six.

46% of developers name it their most-loved tool. Double Cursor. Five times GitHub Copilot. Coding is now 51% of all enterprise generative AI usage, the highest-value category in the market per recent developer surveys.

The consensus on Anthropic was that it wins on safety and model quality. Claude is smarter, more careful, better at long context. Enterprise pays the premium. That thesis holds. The product moving the profit line is a CLI that developers open before writing a single line.

Microsoft paid $7.5 billion for GitHub in 2018 to own the developer tooling layer. It is building Copilot on top of that distribution today. Anthropic launched a terminal tool and reached $2.5 billion ARR before most developer tools startups finished their Series A.

The company that was supposed to win on research is winning on a terminal.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people think of Anthropic as the safety-first lab, the one that published the Constitutional AI paper and pushed responsible scaling policies. The more I looked at this week's revenue numbers, the more I realized the frame that actually explains the business is simpler: they went developer-native earlier and more completely than anyone else.

Claude Code is at $2.5 billion in annualized revenue. That is roughly 23% of total company revenue from a terminal CLI that launched about a year ago. Anthropic is projecting its first-ever operating profit this quarter, $559 million on $10.9 billion in revenue. The operating profit exists largely because of a product that was not originally framed as the core business.

The deeper pattern is about where enterprise AI value is actually settling. Coding is 51% of all enterprise generative AI usage, the highest-value category by a significant margin. Developers are the fastest-deciding, highest-paying buyers in the market. The companies that built tools for them first, and built those tools where developers already work, are the ones posting profits.

I am not yet sure whether Claude Code holds its position as GitHub Copilot scales on Microsoft's distribution. That competition is real and coming. But the Q2 numbers suggest Anthropic found the value layer before the market had named it.

ideas.title: Circle Just Built the Payment Layer for a Non-Human Economy
ideas.trend: Circle launched Agent Stack on May 11 with agent wallets, nanopayments at $0.000001 per transaction, and an agent marketplace for USDC-powered AI commerce
ideas.consensus: Stablecoins are for crypto traders and B2B cross-border remittances
ideas.angle: Circle built the first payment infrastructure formally designed for non-human economic actors; traditional rails (Stripe minimum $0.10, card networks requiring a cardholder) cannot serve sub-cent machine commerce; Circle owns the default rail before the market realizes it needs one

content_pack.x_longform:
Circle built the first financial infrastructure designed for non-human customers.

Every bank account and every payment card in the global system was built for a human with a legal identity. AI agents have neither. Circle's Agent Stack, launched earlier this month, gives agents programmable wallets with policy-controlled guardrails, nanopayments settling at $0.000001 per transaction, and a marketplace where agents discover and hire other agents in USDC.

Stripe's minimum transaction cost sits around $0.10. Card networks require a cardholder of record. Those rails structurally cannot serve sub-cent machine commerce. Circle built rails that can.
content_pack.x_thread:
1/ Circle built the first financial infrastructure designed for non-human customers. [thread]

2/ Agent Stack launched earlier this month. Agent Wallets: permissionless, policy-controlled, no KYC required. Agents hold, send, and manage USDC within predefined guardrails. First time that has been formally built for non-humans.

3/ Nanopayments: gas-free USDC transfers settling at $0.000001 per transaction. Stripe's minimum is ~$0.10. Card networks require a cardholder of record. Traditional rails cannot serve sub-cent machine commerce.

4/ Agent Marketplace: a directory where agents discover and pay for other agents' services in USDC. Agents hire agents. The economy settles on-chain.

5/ Every payment system ever built assumed a human with a legal identity at one end. KYC eliminates non-human actors from traditional rails. Circle is the first institution to formally step outside that assumption.

6/ The infrastructure window is real. Whoever builds the default payment rails for AI commerce tends to keep them. Circle is first with a production system.
content_pack.substack_draft:
$0.000001. That number is doing a lot of work in Circle's announcement this month.

Circle launched something called Agent Stack: programmable wallets for AI agents, nanopayments settling at a fraction of a cent per transaction, and a marketplace where agents discover and pay for other agents in USDC. The launch is quiet by AI news standards. Most of the coverage this week is about SpaceX's IPO filing and Anthropic's revenue numbers. But what Circle built is structurally more interesting to me as a payments question than either of those stories.

Every financial system that exists was designed for a human who has a legal identity, a government-issued document, and a bank account. KYC requirements eliminate non-human actors from the traditional rails. Card networks require a cardholder of record. Stripe's minimum transaction cost makes sub-cent payments economically unworkable at scale. Circle is the first institution to formally step outside that assumption and build infrastructure for a different customer class: software that earns and spends.

Whether the agent-to-agent economy materializes at the scale being projected is the real open question. The nanopayment use case, agents paying fractions of a cent per API call or per task, requires a level of autonomous economic activity that is still early. But the infrastructure window is real, and it closes once a default rail gets established.
